Optimization and Regularization

CSE 30124 · Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
William Theisen · University of Notre Dame
Optimization and Regularization01

Problems with OLS

Last chapter we found the best line through Notre Dame's games by writing down a loss (the SSE), picturing it as a bowl over the weights, and solving for the bottom of the bowl. That gave us Ordinary Least Squares, ωT = (XT X)−1 XT y, and a line worth about 9 points per 100 yards.

Unfortunately, the chapter ended on two problems. The first is the inverse. With 119 features XT X is a 119 by 119 matrix, and inverting it takes on the order of 1193 steps. Worse, when one feature can be built from the others (total yards is just pass yards plus rush yards) the inverse doesn't exist at all.

The second is overfitting. Our degree-8 curve fit the 13 games from 2012 with an MSE of 15, then missed the 2013 games with an MSE of 9,553.

The first problem is about how we find our weights. The second is about which weights we might want in the first place.

Optimization and Regularization02

An iterative method

Instead of jumping straight to the bottom of the bowl, we can walk downhill a little at a time.

\omega \leftarrow \lk{step}{\omega - \lk{alpha}{\alpha}\,\lk{grad}{\frac{\partial ℒ}{\partial \omega}}}
[6.1]
one step of gradient descent
XQ𝛚←XQ𝛚−α∂XQ𝓛∂XQ𝛚
1

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([14, 20, 31, 40, 49])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
w = np.zeros(2)
alpha = 0.01
for step in range(5000):
grad = -2 * X.T @ (y - X @ w) # dL/dw
w = w - alpha * grad # one step downhill
print(w.round(2))
Output
[-5.2  9. ]

Here ω is the whole list of weights, ∂ℒ/∂ω is the same gradient we set to zero last chapter, and α is the learning rate, how big a step we take each time. Rather than solving for where the gradient is zero, we keep stepping against it until it is. This is called gradient descent, and notice that there's no inverse anywhere. Each step costs a couple of matrix multiplications, so a million features is slow but no longer impossible.

Optimization and Regularization · Optimization03

The Learning Rate

Starting from weights of 0 on our five games, here's how close each learning rate gets after 100 steps. The bottom of the bowl (ω0 = −5.2, ω1 = 9.0) has an SSE of 4.8.

αω0ω1SSE
0.0010.987.6226.0
0.005−1.168.1013.9
0.01−2.838.477.9

A bigger step gets there faster, until it doesn't. At α = 0.02 each step jumps clean over the bottom of the bowl and lands higher up the other side, and every step after that makes it worse (by step 1,000 every weight is nan). For these five games anything above 0.0106 blows up. Picking the learning rate is most of the work in getting gradient descent to behave.

Unfortunately, gradient descent only fixes the cost. It walks to the bottom of the same bowl OLS solved for, so it inherits whatever is wrong with that bottom. Give it total, pass and rush yards and the bowl stretches into a long, nearly flat valley (total yards is the sum of the other two in all but one game). The bottom of that valley is at weights of −64, +72 and +74 points per 100 yards, and gradient descent would find the same weights, just very slowly.

Optimization and Regularization · Optimization04

Overfitting

Those weights should look familiar. Last chapter's degree-8 curve fit the 13 games from 2012 almost perfectly and then fell apart on 2013, and its weights were the same kind of thing, enormous and cancelling each other out.

Linear regressions are prone to overfitting because nothing in the SSE cares how big the weights get. If a weight of 1.9 million shaves a little more error off the training games, OLS will happily use it.

Optimization and Regularization · Optimization05

Large Weights

Here are the biggest weights (leaving out the intercept) for each of last chapter's polynomials, fit to the 2012 games and tested on 2013:

ModelBiggest weightMSE on 2012MSE on 2013
line (degree 1)8.43956
degree 25.93956
degree 42433565
degree 81.9 million159,553

The weights and the 2013 error climb together. To bend through every 2012 game the degree-8 curve needs each weight to almost exactly cancel the ones next to it, and that balance only holds where the 2012 games were. Our one 2013 game with fewer yards than any 2012 game (220) gets a prediction of −330 points.

A model that needs enormous, finely balanced weights is almost always fitting the noise. So the obvious fix is to make big weights cost us something.

Optimization and Regularization · Optimization06

Regularization: L1 and L2

To help prevent overfitting when using linear regressions, we can perform a technique called regularization.

The goal of regularization is to encourage models to learn the broader patterns within the data rather than memorizing it.

Regularization does this by adding a second term to the loss that measures how big the weights are. There are two common ways to measure it, adding up the squared weights (called L2, or ridge) or adding up their absolute values (L1, or LASSO).

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization07

Formalizations of regularization

There are two ways to formalize regularization:

  • As a cost (penalty) placed on the weights
  • As a budget (constraint) for the weights
Optimization and Regularization · Regularization08

Regularization as a cost

When we formalize regularization as a cost, we modify the loss function such that increasing the weights incurs a "cost".

We use an argument called λ to determine how heavily the cost is weighed. A larger λ increases the cost.

ℒ(\omega) = \text{SSE}(\omega) + \lambda \sum_j \omega_j^2 ℒ(\omega) = \text{SSE}(\omega) + \lambda \sum_j |\omega_j|
[6.2]
L2 as a cost
XQ𝓛(XQ𝛚)=SSE(XQ𝛚)+XQ𝛌∑jXQ𝛚𝐣2
[6.3]
L1 as a cost
XQ𝓛(XQ𝛚)=SSE(XQ𝛚)+XQ𝛌∑j|XQ𝛚𝐣|

With λ = 0 both are just the SSE again, so OLS is the special case where we don't care at all how big the weights get.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization09

Regularization as a cost, increasing λ

A larger λ increases the cost of our weights, typically resulting in the optimum being pulled closer to the origin.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization10

Ridge on the 2012 Season

Here is last chapter's degree-8 polynomial fit to the 2012 games twice, once with plain OLS and once with ridge at λ = 1 (the intercept left out of the penalty):

λBiggest weightMSE on 2012MSE on 2013
0 (plain OLS)1.9 million159,553
12.33255
1000.133457

The penalty costs us a little on 2012 and saves us almost everything on 2013. At λ = 1 the degree-8 curve even does slightly better on 2013 than the plain line did (55 against 56), with nine weights instead of two. Push λ up to 100 and the curve flattens back toward a line, so λ is a dial between variance and bias.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization11

Ridge and the Inverse

Ridge also fixes our first problem, almost by accident. Take the gradient of the ridge loss, set it to zero like we did for OLS, and the only change is a λ added down the diagonal:

\omega\T = (X\T X + \lk{lam}{\lambda I})^{-1} X\T y
[6.4]
ridge, solved in one step
XQ𝛚T=(XTX+XQ𝛌I)−1XTXQ𝐲

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([14, 20, 31, 40, 49])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
lam = 1.0
I = np.eye(2)
I[0, 0] = 0 # leave the intercept unpenalized
w = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * I, X.T @ y)
print(w.round(2))
Output
[-1.93  8.18]

Adding any positive λ to the diagonal guarantees the inverse exists, so the flat valley turns back into a bowl with one bottom. In practice we usually leave the intercept ω0 out of the penalty (there's no reason to push the average score toward 0), so the top-left entry of I becomes a 0.

Back to total, pass and rush yards from the learning rate page. Plain OLS gave us weights of −64, +72 and +74. Ridge with λ = 1 gives +5.9 on total yards, +2.0 on pass yards and +3.9 on rush yards. The predictions barely change (100 passing yards is still worth about 8 points and 100 rushing yards about 10), but now every weight is positive and none of them are absurd.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization12

Regularization as a budget

When we formalize regularization as a budget, we constrain our loss function such that the weights chosen must remain within "budget".

\min_\omega \ \text{SSE}(\omega) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_j \omega_j^2 \le t \min_\omega \ \text{SSE}(\omega) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_j |\omega_j| \le t
L2 as a budget
minXQ𝛚⁡ SSE(XQ𝛚)subject to∑jXQ𝛚𝐣2≤t
L1 as a budget
minXQ𝛚⁡ SSE(XQ𝛚)subject to∑j|XQ𝛚𝐣|≤t
Optimization and Regularization · Regularization13

Regularization as a budget, increasing t

A larger t increases the budget for our weights, typically resulting in the optimum being closer to the unconstrained optimum.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization14

Sparsity

Look at the L1 row of the cost pictures. At λ = 3 the star lands exactly on one of the axes, so one of the two weights is exactly 0. A model with weights of exactly 0 is called sparse. The budget pictures show why it happens: the L1 budget is a diamond, and the loss bowl almost always touches a diamond first at one of its corners, which sit right on the axes. The L2 budget is a circle with no corners, so its star gets pulled in close to an axis but never quite lands on it.

The cost and the budget aren't really two different ideas, they're the same problem written two ways. For every budget t there's some λ that puts the star in exactly the same spot (proving it takes Lagrange multipliers). A big λ is a small budget, and a small λ is a big one.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization15

Feature Selection

A weight of exactly 0 means that feature is out of the model entirely, so L1 is doing feature selection for us for free. Let's give it something to select. Here are seven things from Notre Dame's box score: total yards, first downs, turnovers, penalties, third-down conversions, time of possession and number of plays.

Plain OLS uses all seven and explains 64% of the variation in points. LASSO with a moderate λ keeps exactly two of them, total yards (about 7.9 points per 100 yards) and turnovers (about −1.9 points each), and still explains 61%. The other five weights are exactly 0. Most of what a box score tells you about points, it turns out, is how far you moved the ball and how often you gave it away.

One practical detail: before using LASSO we rescale every feature to the same spread. Otherwise a feature measured in big units (yards) and one measured in small units (turnovers) get penalized very differently for the same amount of usefulness.

sklearn has both. One annoying detail: sklearn calls λ alpha, which has nothing to do with the learning rate from gradient descent.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
games = pd.read_csv("nd_football.csv")
cols = ["nd_total_yards", "nd_pass_yards",
"nd_rush_yards"]
X = games[cols] / 100
y = games["nd_points"]
ols = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
ridge = Ridge(alpha=1).fit(X, y) # alpha is λ here
print(ols.coef_.round(1))
print(ridge.coef_.round(1))
Output
[-64.4  72.4  74.2]
[5.9 2.  3.9]

Same predictions as OLS, sensible weights, exactly as on the inverse page.

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
games = pd.read_csv("nd_football.csv")
stats = ["nd_total_yards", "nd_first_downs",
"nd_turnovers", "nd_penalties",
"nd_third_down_conv", "nd_possession_min",
"nd_plays"]
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(games[stats])
y = games["nd_points"]
lasso = Lasso(alpha=1).fit(X, y)
for name, w in zip(stats, lasso.coef_):
print(f"{name:20s} {w + 0:6.2f}")
Output
nd_total_yards         8.16
nd_first_downs         0.00
nd_turnovers          -2.29
nd_penalties           0.00
nd_third_down_conv     0.00
nd_possession_min      0.00
nd_plays               0.00

These LASSO weights are per standard deviation (that's what StandardScaler did), so compare them to each other rather than to the 9 points per 100 yards from before.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization18

Maximum Likelihood, Revisited

Last chapter we saw that least squares is maximum likelihood in disguise. Regularization fits into the same picture, with one extra term.

The setup is an assumption about the noise. Every game's score is the line plus some noise, and the noise is Gaussian with spread σ: yi = ŷi + εi with εi ~ N(0, σ2). MLE picks the weights that make the scores we saw most likely, and taking the negative log turns that product of bell curves into a sum of squares:

\hat \omega_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_\omega\ p(y \mid \omega) \text{take } -\log = \arg\min_\omega\ \frac{\text{SSE}(\omega)}{2\sigma^2} = \arg\min_\omega\ \text{SSE}(\omega)
[6.5]
MLE
XQ𝛚𝐌𝐋𝐄ˆ=arg⁡maxXQ𝛚⁡ p(XQ𝐲|XQ𝛚)
↓take −log⁡
=arg⁡minXQ𝛚⁡ SSE(XQ𝛚)2σ2=arg⁡minXQ𝛚⁡ SSE(XQ𝛚)
Optimization and Regularization · Regularization19

Adding a prior

We could also say which weights we expected before seeing any games (a prior, p(ω)), and ask for the most likely weights given the data. By Bayes' rule that means multiplying the prior in. If we believe each weight is probably near 0, a Gaussian prior ωj ~ N(0, τ2), its negative log is one more sum of squares:

\hat \omega_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\omega\ p(y \mid \omega)\,p(\omega) \text{take } -\log = \arg\min_\omega\ \frac{\text{SSE}(\omega)}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_j \omega_j^2 \text{multiply by } 2\sigma^2 = \arg\min_\omega\ \text{SSE}(\omega) + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\sum_j \omega_j^2
MAP
XQ𝛚𝐌𝐀𝐏ˆ=arg⁡maxXQ𝛚⁡ p(XQ𝐲|XQ𝛚)p(XQ𝛚)
↓take −log⁡
=arg⁡minXQ𝛚⁡ SSE(XQ𝛚)2σ2+12τ2∑jXQ𝛚𝐣2
↓multiply by 2σ2
[6.6]
=arg⁡minXQ𝛚⁡ SSE(XQ𝛚)+σ2τ2∑jXQ𝛚𝐣2

That's the ridge loss [6.2] with λ = σ2/τ2. So λ is how noisy we think the data is, divided by how big we think the weights are. Our yards-and-turnovers line misses by about 7.7 points a game (σ2 ≈ 60), so if we expected weights of about ±5 (τ = 5) we'd get λ ≈ 2.4. A flat prior (τ → ∞) sends λ to 0 and MAP back to MLE. A Laplace prior, p(ωj) ∝ e−|ωj|/b, gives λ Σ|ωj| instead, which is LASSO.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization20

MAP estimation

L1 and L2 regularization are a form of MAP Estimation.

MAP stands for Maximum A Posteriori which is a Bayesian approach for applying a prior to our weights.

So both kinds of regularization are a prior in disguise. Ridge is a belief that the weights are probably small, LASSO a sharper belief that piles up right at 0, and λ is how strongly we believe it compared to the data. Regularization is really just us telling the model what we expected ahead of time.

Optimization and Regularization · Regularization21
